title: The Best Preparation for a Digital Future Is an Analogue Education Alliance for Responsible Citizenship Conference, London, June 22, 2026
author: Sophie Winkleman
source: First Fish Chronicles (firstfish.substack.com), July 10, 2026 — remarks delivered at the
summary: Actress and screen-use campaigner Sophie Winkleman argues that the rush to put children's education on screens — first through EdTech, now through AI — is a well-marketed mistake, and that the best preparation for a digital future is a deliberately analogue education. She opens with a headteacher whose pupils had lost the capacity to 'go and play,' their imaginations deactivated by constant low-level device stimulation, and builds outward to a systemic critique: roughly one million British children now spend nearly every lesson on a screen, while parents watch headaches, lost focus, disrupted sleep, and short-sightedness accumulate. Her central move is to collapse the supposed distinction between harmful social media and 'educational' technology, noting that the streaks, rewards, and notifications restricted on social platforms are the very slot-machine mechanics now baked into maths, language, and reading apps — features that exist to drive engagement, not learning. She marshals evidence for the physical superiority of analogue learning: material read on paper implants more deeply than the same text on screen, handwriting lights up the whole brain where typing leaves it dark, and a 3,000-student PISA experiment found paper-based work scored the equivalent of six months' extra schooling. Turning to AI, she argues that children who outsource the 'lengthy, fibrous, but ultimately joyful journey' of learning skip a crucial phase of cognitive development — likening AI-in-schools to telling a baby not to bother crawling — and warns that hallucination, sycophancy, and engagement-maximisation are core properties of the technology, not teething problems. The piece closes on an equity and civilisational note: elite schools like Winchester are going 'paper-first' while poorer children get chatbot tutors, and, invoking Postman's reading of Huxley, she insists adults must not inflict on children the surrender of their own capacity to think.
points: Winkleman's core argument dissolves the line between 'harmful' social media and 'educational' technology: the streaks, daily rewards, and endless notifications restricted on social platforms are the identical slot-machine mechanics now built into maths, language, and even reading apps — present because they drive engagement, which is what the business model requires, not because they improve learning.

The case for analogue is grounded in neuroscience and measurement, not nostalgia: paper reading implants material more deeply than screen reading, Audrey van der Meer's scans show the brain 'lit up like a Christmas tree' during handwriting and 'dark as a cellar' during typing, and John Jerrim's 3,000-student PISA experiment found paper-based students scored 20 points higher — about six months of extra schooling.

Her AI critique is developmental: children who let AI do the thinking skip the effortful 'crawling phase' of cognitive maturation, and because AI hallucinates, flatters, and is engineered to keep users coming back, these are 'core properties of the technology,' not bugs to be patched — making 'deploy now, test later' uniquely dangerous in education.

The equity reversal is the sharpest institutional point: EdTech was sold as a way to close the attainment gap, but elite schools (e.g., Winchester College) are adopting stringent 'paper-first' policies while Britain's poorest children are handed chatbot tutors and 'digital slop' — the technology is widening the gap it promised to bridge.

The constructive prescription, borrowed from futurist James Poulter and consultant Emily Cherkin, is 'Tech Ed, not Ed Tech': teach how technology works in dedicated technology lessons, and return to books, handwriting, and human teachers for everything else — protecting the teacher-pupil relationship as a load-bearing factor in academic success.
quotes: She came to realise that these children did not have the capacity to ‘go and play’; they couldn’t create their own fun, their own entertainment, so accustomed were they to receiving entertainment via their devices.
One million children in Britain spend nearly every lesson on a screen. Welcome to the world of EdTech.

The social media design features deemed harmful enough to restrict for children - the streaks, the daily rewards, the endless notifications – are the very same features found in EdTech apps. These are slot-machine tactics – the same unpredictable reward which keeps an adult scrolling now built into maths, languages and even reading apps.
Material read from a page in a book implants in the brain more profoundly than the exact same material read from a screen. We are physical beings, we must learn physically.
Half the students conducted all their work on paper, half did all their work on a computer. The paper-based group scored twenty points higher – the equivalent of six months’ extra schooling.
Immediate relief in exchange for long-term dependency seems to be AI’s defining trade-off: an instant elevation of results, twinned with a long-term dwindling of capability.

Many tech giants send their own children to low-tech schools; aware that the most highly-prized human capital in the coming era will be the ability to think - deeply, knowledgeably and originally; to be the best of what a human can be, not a pale imitation of AI.
